During a wildfire, surrounding dry forests burn quickly. Beavers can help reduce the spread and severity of these wildfires by building dams and creating wetlands that retain moisture and keep the vegetation moist, and the saturated soil and water-rich plants create a bright green zone that resists catching fire. These wetlands also become vital emergency shelters during the fire and critical survival habitats after burn, providing food and shelter when the surrounding forest is destroyed. When a wildfire breaks out, large animals like deer, bears, and birds flee toward beaver ponds, and smaller animals like amphibians and rodents hide in the moist mud or swim in the deep water. They act as natural firebreaks, creating wet, fire-resistant zones that mitigate fire spread, shelter wildlife, and help ecosystems recover after fires.

When beavers build a dam across a stream, they slow down the rushing water and create a “beaver pond”.  Instead of letting rainwater and melting snow rush quickly downstream and out of the area, the dam acts like a speed bump. The water piles up behind it, giving it nowhere to go. Due to the water now moving slowly, it pools up and has time to sink deep into the soil. This water gets trapped underground and creates something scientists call a “water table.”

### Beaver Data
The beaver observation data is from iNaturalist.org and was collected from 1997-2026. It is restricted to the geographical area of California. Each entry represents one reported beaver sighting. iNaturalist is a website that allows people to record observations and classify them. People can upload pictures and locations of observed plants and animals and others on the website will help classify them into species. We requested all the observations of the North American Beaver (castor canadensis). 

When we got the data, it was all objects, thus we had to change each column to a reasonable data type. Each entry has an ID, date observed, time observed, quality of the observation, description written by the observer, if the observed animal is wild, a location description from the observer, a longitude and latitude, and species. Longitude and latitude became floating type and time observed became datetime type. There are 2961 entries in this database. 

Some issues with this data source is that it relies on people observing and photographing beavers or evidence of beavers. This means that more beavers will be seen in populated areas than underpopulated areas. This is why we will also be using the reported habitat of the American Beaver by the California Department of Fish and Wildlife. This is just a shape with the reported habitats of beavers. 

### Fire Data
The fire data is from the California Historical Fire Database by the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection. Each entry represents a different fire. In order to be recorded, a fire must be a wildland timber fire greater than 10 acres, brush fire greater than 50 acres, grass fire greater than 300 acres, destroy 3 or more residential or commercial structures, or result in a fatality. Thus, this database will not include tiny fires that cause very little damage. 

Each entry has the state where the fire started, year, agency responsible for the fire, name of the fire, date of fire discovery, date of fire containment, cause, acres damaged, and an ID for the fire. There are a few fires that started in Oregon, Nevada, and Arizona that spread to California. There are 18,064 entries in this database spanning from 1950-2025.

```{python python-setup}
import requests
```

```{python importing}
import os
import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd

beaver_range_path = os.path.expanduser('~/courses/csds133/cas393/csds133-26fa-cas393/5-FinalProject/data/American_Beaver_Range_-_CWHR_M112_[ds1899] (1).geojson')
fire_path = os.path.expanduser('~/courses/csds133/cas393/csds133-26fa-cas393/5-FinalProject/data/California_Historic_Fire_Perimeters_6966767162278220358 (1).geojson')
beavers_csv_path = os.path.expanduser('~/courses/csds133/cas393/csds133-26fa-cas393/5-FinalProject/data/i_natural_beavers.csv')

# Load boundaries & fires
ca_bdf = gpd.read_file(beaver_range_path)
ca_fire = gpd.read_file(fire_path)

# Download state boundaries
states_url = "https://www2.census.gov/geo/tiger/GENZ2024/shp/cb_2024_us_state_20m.zip"
states = gpd.read_file(states_url)
ca = states[states["NAME"] == "California"]

ca_beavers_df = pd.read_csv(beavers_csv_path)

# Convert types
ca_beavers_df['longitude'] = pd.to_numeric(ca_beavers_df['longitude'], errors='coerce')
ca_beavers_df['latitude'] = pd.to_numeric(ca_beavers_df['latitude'], errors='coerce')
ca_beavers_df['observed_on'] = pd.to_datetime(ca_beavers_df['observed_on'], errors='coerce')
ca_beavers_df['time_observed_at'] = pd.to_datetime(ca_beavers_df['time_observed_at'], errors='coerce')

# Drop rows with missing coordinates before creating geometry
ca_beavers_df = ca_beavers_df.dropna(subset=['longitude', 'latitude'])

# Fix fire dates
ca_fire['ALARM_DATE'] = pd.to_datetime(ca_fire['ALARM_DATE'], errors='coerce')
ca_fire['CONT_DATE'] = pd.to_datetime(ca_fire['CONT_DATE'], errors='coerce')
```

```{python graph-ca-map}

from matplotlib.patches import Patch
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D

)

    Patch(facecolor='lightseagreen', alpha=0.3, label='Beaver Habitats'),
    Patch(facecolor='coral', alpha=0.6, label='Reported Fires'),

           markerfacecolor='darkgreen', markersize=6)
]

bx.set_title("Beavers and Fires in California", fontsize=20)
bx.set_xlabel("Longitude", fontsize=18)
bx.set_ylabel("Latitude", fontsize=18)

bx.legend(handles=legend_elements,loc='upper right', fontsize=10)

plt.show()
```

Figures are large so that we could copy them into the presentation.
```{python seasonality-in-fires}
# Extract temporal features from ALARM_DATE
ca_fire['Month'] = ca_fire['ALARM_DATE'].dt.strftime('%B')
ca_fire['Year'] = ca_fire['ALARM_DATE'].dt.year

# Order of months for plotting
month_order = ['January', 'February', 'March', 'April', 'May', 'June',
               'July', 'August', 'September', 'October', 'November', 'December']

# Create subplots to show both seasonality and yearly trends
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 12))

# 1. Fire frequency by Month (Seasonality)
sns.countplot(
    data=ca_fire,
    x='Month',
    order=month_order,
    ax=axes[0]
)
axes[0].set_title('California Fire Occurrences by Month')
axes[0].set_xlabel('Month')
axes[0].set_ylabel('Number of Fires')
axes[0].tick_params(axis='x', rotation=45)

# 2. Fire frequency by Year (Trends - focusing on recent decades for clarity)
recent_fires = ca_fire[ca_fire['Year'] >= 1980]
yearly_counts = recent_fires.groupby('Year').size().reset_index(name='Count')

sns.lineplot(
    data=yearly_counts,
    x='Year',
    y='Count',
    ax=axes[1],
    marker='o',
    color='red'
)
axes[1].set_title('California Fire Occurrences by Year (Since 1980)')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Year')
axes[1].set_ylabel('Number of Fires')
axes[1].grid(True, linestyle='--', alpha=0.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
